notes.meaning: The psalm opens by inviting God's people to sing to the Lord together, with real joy. God is called the "Rock of our salvation." That means He is the firm, safe ground our rescue stands on. Many readers have also seen Christ here as that Rock.

We are to come before God with thanks, not cold or slow, but eager. The word for "enter" can carry the idea of hurrying to meet Him. Joy is as much a part of true worship as seriousness. Worship rests mainly on praise from the heart, not on empty ritual.

Here is the first reason to praise: the Lord is a great King over all so-called gods. These include the idols people make, which are really nothing. Some also see angels and earthly rulers here, who are all under His rule.

The whole world belongs to God, from the deepest places to the highest mountain tops. The sea and the dry land are His because He made them. Being the Maker of all makes Him the owner of all. He still holds and rules everything by His care, which is often called His "providence."

The call to worship comes again, now with humble awe. Three words are used: worship (lying face down), bow down, and kneel. Together they mean giving our whole selves to God. Our bodies should show the respect our hearts feel before the Lord who made us.

The deepest reason to worship is that He is our God, and we belong to Him like sheep to a shepherd. He feeds, leads, and protects us with His own hand. Christians see Christ as the Good Shepherd of His church. The last line begins a warning: hear His voice today, because the chance will not last forever.

Don't let your heart grow hard and stubborn. Meribah means "quarrel" and Massah means "testing." These were names given to a place where Israel complained against God over water in the desert (Exodus 17). Their story is written to warn us not to follow their steps.

Now God Himself speaks. Israel "tested" Him by doubting and demanding new proofs, even after seeing His mighty works of mercy and judgment. Not trusting God after all He has shown is a kind of testing Him.

For forty years in the desert, that generation grieved God. Their problem was not mainly in their heads but in their hearts, which kept wandering. They knew God's ways well enough, but they did not love them or walk in them.

God swore that this generation would not enter His "rest," the promised land of Canaan. Only Joshua and Caleb did; the rest died in the desert. Hebrews 3–4 uses this to warn Christians. It also points to a deeper rest God gives to those who believe, begun now and made complete in heaven.
